title: Verification: grid convergence and manufactured solutions
summary: Two panels: error against grid spacing on log-log axes with the observed order, and a quantity of interest against grid spacing with a Richardson extrapolation and a grid-convergence-index band. It asks whether the solver solves its equations at the expected rate.

media.alt: Two panels: log-log plot of error against grid spacing with a slope-two reference line and printed observed order, and a plot of a quantity against grid spacing with an extrapolated value and a shaded band.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Is the solver right?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: x grid spacing h in m (log), y error norm ||u - u_ex||_2 (log, dimensionless). Right: x grid spacing h (log), y quantity of interest f (linear) against h.
look_at: Are the points on a straight line, and is it parallel to the ideal-order dashed line?
What observed order p is printed, and does it match the scheme's design order?
Does f(h) approach one value as h falls?
How wide is the GCI band around the extrapolated value?
read_the_figure.proves: If the observed order equals the formal order and the error falls like h^p, the discretisation is correct (code verification). The GCI band gives an uncertainty for a quantity on the finest grid. It says nothing about modelling error: that is validation.
if_wrong: Observed order below the design order: a bug, a boundary treatment of lower order, or not yet asymptotic.
Points that wander, not a line: the grids are not in the asymptotic range, or not geometrically similar.
Three grids with a refinement ratio near 1: the order cannot be extracted.

terms.meaning: Showing that the equations are solved right (code correctness). Different from validation, which asks whether they are the right equations.
The slope p of log error against log h, measured from the results.
Choose an exact solution, insert it in the equations to get a source term, and measure the error against it.
Estimate of the grid-independent value from two grids and the observed order.
A safety-factor-weighted estimate of the relative discretisation error on the fine grid.

remember: error ~ C h^p. Slope on log-log = p.
p = ln[(f3 - f2)/(f2 - f1)] / ln r for three grids with ratio r.
GCI = Fs |f1 - f2| / (|f1| (r^p - 1)), Fs = 1.25 for three grids.
Verification compares with an exact or manufactured solution; the GCI is for real problems without one.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Left: position encodes grid spacing (log) and error (log). Teal circles joined by a line are the solver, an amber dashed line shows the ideal slope. The bold teal text prints the fitted order. Right: blue squares show the quantity of interest on each grid, a dotted amber line is the extrapolated value, and an amber band is the GCI around it.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: If the error is C h^p, then ln e is a straight line in ln h with slope p: the exponent becomes a slope and the eye can test it against a parallel reference. The right panel answers the practical question for a real problem: how much do I trust the number on my finest grid. Together they say the code is correct and give an error bar.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: What order is observed? The printed value p = 2.03, and the teal points lie on the amber dashed line of order 2 from h = 0.4 (error about 0.15) to h = 0.05 (about 2e-3). Q2: Does f converge? Yes: f falls from about 1.074 at h = 0.4 to 1.018, 1.004 and 1.001 at the finer grids, towards the dotted extrapolated value 1.000. Q3: How big is the GCI? The amber band is 0.13 percent of f on the finest grid, which is the claimed discretisation uncertainty there.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Observed order and GCI band: the first proves the formal order, the second gives the uncertainty. If either is missing the figure supports only a qualitative claim of convergence.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Two points always lie on a line, and three points in a narrow range of h fit almost any slope. The error needs an exact solution; for real problems only the right panel is possible, and it relies on the grids being in the asymptotic range. Fs = 1.25 is a convention, not a bound. A single quantity at one point can converge while others do not. Non-monotone convergence breaks the formula.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A table of h, f, p and GCI is often clearer. The error against the number of cells in 3D is more honest about cost. A convergence plot of several quantities on one panel shows which converge slowly.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a fifth finer grid, add error bars of the extrapolation, and a table of p between successive pairs.

worked.title: Order and GCI from the right panel
worked.problem: Read f = 1.0183, 1.0044, 1.0011 for h = 0.2, 0.1, 0.05 (ratio r = 2). Find p, f_ext and the GCI on the finest grid.
worked.answer: p about 2.07, f_ext about 1.0001, GCI about 0.13 percent: consistent with the figure's printed 2.03 and 0.13 percent.

checks.q: What does the slope of the left panel mean?
checks.hint: Take the log of error = C h^p.
checks.answer: The observed order p of the method.

checks.q: Error 4e-2 at h = 0.2 and 1e-2 at h = 0.1. Order?
The observed order drifts from 2.0 to 1.4 on the finest grid. What do you check?
checks.answer: Check that the iterative convergence (F10.9) is tight enough on the fine grid and that a first-order boundary treatment is not dominating the error as h falls.
